prompt: Describe a time you turned an ambiguous request into an actionable goal. What did you personally clarify and how did you know it helped?
provenance: Original synthetic answer authored for mockr; not an actual candidate or human-scored label.

transcript.answer: During a fictional neighborhood science fair, five organizers disagreed about what better registration meant. Some wanted more fields; others wanted fewer abandoned registrations. We had two weeks and one volunteer developer.

I owned turning the request into a measurable proposal, not making the final policy decision. I agreed with the organizer that success meant fewer incomplete registrations without collecting extra personal information.

I mapped the existing flow with two organizers, counted completion events on a synthetic trial, and asked four volunteers to narrate their experience. I proposed clearer required-field labels instead of adding profile fields. I documented the alternative and its privacy cost so the organizer could make an informed decision.

Across two small synthetic trial groups of thirty, completion rose from eighteen to twenty-four. This was directional, not causal proof: participants differed. We shipped the label change and reviewed incomplete attempts weekly instead of claiming the entire gain as my impact.

I would randomize the next trial and predefine a success threshold. In the next planning discussion I separated the desired outcome from the proposed feature before estimating work. That kept the team focused on evidence and avoided collecting unnecessary data.
